name: Pirsch
tagline: Collect cookieless page views and custom events with compact dashboards

pricing.notes: Typical entry monthly price; page-view volume changes the tier.

tiers.name: Standard
tiers.limits: At the displayed 10,000-pageview level: 10,000 monthly pageviews, 50 websites, unlimited members, and unlimited data retention
tiers.notes: Annual equivalent follows the page's stated $12 yearly saving: $60/year. Price rises with the selected monthly pageview allowance.

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: At the displayed 10,000-pageview level: 10,000 monthly pageviews, unlimited websites/members/retention, plus funnels, teams, A/B testing, segmentation, custom domains and white labeling
tiers.notes: Annual equivalent follows the page's stated $24 yearly saving: $120/year. Price rises with the selected monthly pageview allowance.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Variable traffic with unlimited websites/members/retention; managed cloud or on-premise, SAML SSO and raw-data access

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; 30-day no-card trial; prices exclude tax
pricing.hiddenCosts: Custom events and 10% of session-extension events count against the pageview quota, and deleted domains keep counting until reset. At the cap, dashboard access is limited and collection continues only 5 more days unless you upgrade.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Pirsch, collect cookieless page views and custom events with compact dashboards. The hard boundary is hosted reliability, privacy operations, apis, email reports, and scale, plus data pipeline reliability and analytical depth.
coreLoopDIY: Collect cookieless first-party page views and custom events, answer a small set of product questions with compact dashboards, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: hosted reliability, privacy operations, APIs, email reports, and scale
moatNotes: data pipeline reliability and analytical depth
ongoingBurden: event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Pirsch because teams pay because analytics must keep collecting and remain trustworthy while the product changes underneath it. The recurring cost buys event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Umami
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source privacy-focused web analytics platform.

alternatives.name: GoatCounter
alternatives.desc: The tiny option: page views, paths and referrers without a product-management department.

facts.install: Create a hosted account or run the single static binary or Docker image
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted instance uses SQLite by default or PostgreSQL; the hosted service stores analytics on GoatCounter's infrastructure and supports JSON and CSV exports
facts.gapVsPaid: Its custom-event, conversion, API and integration capabilities are shallower than Pirsch's.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted use; self-hosting needs a reachable binary or container plus a public URL and TLS

alternatives.name: Plausible Community Edition
alternatives.desc: Simple cookieless traffic and goals; the Community Edition keeps the dashboard deliberately narrow.

facts.install: Deploy the Community Edition with the official Docker Compose installer
facts.dataFormat: Account and configuration records live in PostgreSQL and analytics events live in ClickHouse on the user's server
facts.gapVsPaid: It covers page views and goals, but self-hosting is heavier and its server-side collection and API story is less polished than Pirsch's.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker Compose, roughly 2 GB of RAM, a domain with DNS and TLS, and backups for PostgreSQL and ClickHouse

alternatives.name: Rybbit
alternatives.desc: A broader cookieless dashboard with events, goals and funnels, still deployable from Compose.

facts.install: Use the hosted service or deploy the free self-hosted edition with Docker Compose
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack uses PostgreSQL for application data, ClickHouse for analytics and Redis for queues and cache; hosted data lives in Rybbit's cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: It is newer and considerably busier, with a heavier stack and a less mature compact dashboard and API than Pirsch.
facts.setupBlocker: The indefinitely free path is self-hosting, which requires Docker Compose, a domain, secrets and enough resources for three data services

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.desc: Cookieless page views and custom events with a compact dashboard and no hosted meter.

facts.install: Create an Umami Cloud account or deploy the Node application with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores analytics and account data in PostgreSQL; Umami Cloud stores it in Umami's managed service
facts.gapVsPaid: It has less emphasis on server-side collection and a less compact API workflow than Pirsch, while self-hosting adds operations.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting requires Docker or Node hosting and a PostgreSQL database

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Standard plan and a single-product first-party analytics DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Pirsch in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: collect cookieless first-party page views and custom events, answer a small set of product questions with compact dashboards, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Ship a lightweight browser SDK for page views and explicit custom events.
Create projects, API keys, environments, event names, and a documented event schema.
Ingest idempotently, filter obvious bots, truncate IP data, and avoid fingerprinting.
Build dashboards for visitors, sessions, funnels, retention, sources, pages, and events.
Expose filters by date, environment, device, country, referrer, and selected properties.
Add retention controls, raw-event export, deletion, health checks, and backup instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out cross-site identity graphs.
Deliberately leave out session replay and automatic DOM capture.
Deliberately leave out warehouse-scale reverse ETL and enterprise governance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
